paras: The Harmony Grove assault on a Black woman was an attack on the night of Saturday, November 21, 1903, about three miles below Harmony Grove in Madison County, Georgia, in which three young white men named Chandler, McGinnis and Fitzpatrick broke into a Black home, carried off a young mother and assaulted her in a field. Warrants were issued for the three men, and one wire report said posses of Black and white men were hunting them with lynching openly promised. Black newspapers and at least one Northern white paper cited the case to answer the claim that sexual assault was a crime of Black men.

According to a special dispatch to the Atlanta Constitution, the three men came about 9 o'clock to the home of a Black family in which there were two women and one man. They broke down the door, threw a baby from the young mother's arms, dragged her out of the house and took her about 100 yards into a field, where they "mercilessly assaulted her." Other reports said she was "criminally assaulted," and one called the crime "torturing" her.

Neighbors heard her screams and came to the field, but the men were armed and kept them at a distance for two hours. The men finally left the woman in a "helpless condition," and she had to be carried home. The dispatch added that the men were said to be under the influence of liquor.

Warrants were issued, and the bailiff or officers searched for the three men, with capture expected the same night. A separate wire from Harmony Grove, run in the Alexandria Gazette under the head "Lynching Party on the Trail," said posses "of both blacks and whites" were searching and that it was "an open statement that lynching will follow the capture of the men." No report of an arrest, a trial or a lynching of the accused was found in the coverage, and the woman is never named.

Georgia and South Carolina papers ran the Harmony Grove text between November 24 and 27 under heads such as "Three White Men Outrage Woman" and "Dragged Woman From Home," calling it "one of the most horrible crimes ever committed in this section." The same text reached Florida in the Ocala Banner and appeared in the Atlanta Constitution's issue of November 30 as "Horrible Crime Is Charged." The Manning Times in South Carolina printed a rewritten version under the head "Ought to Be Hung."

Outside the South, the Springfield Republican judged the case "worth recording" because "the crime" was so often said to be confined to Black men, adding that "the lust of the brutes is not a matter of race" and that the law, not mob violence, should answer it.

Black weeklies took up the story in December and drew a sharper contrast. The St. Paul Appeal quoted the Constitution special and asked, "Have Afro-Americans, ever, at any time, anywhere, committed a crime so horrible as this?" The Cleveland Gazette headed its version "White Brutes" and described the victim as "one of our women," where the white wire had written "a negress." The Wichita Searchlight reprinted the full dispatch on December 19 and closed it with the line "Had this outrage been committed by Negroes on white women they would have been lynched."

The Manning Times rewrite said the men forced the woman into the field "at the point of drawn weapons" and did not mention the broken door or the baby, details given in the Constitution special. Only the Alexandria wire and the Cleveland Gazette's version of it reported Black and white posses and a lynching threat, while the other papers described a search by officers under warrants.

reader.title: Harmony Grove assault on a Black woman (1903)
bases: Three armed white men broke into a Black home, carried off a young mother and assaulted her in a field while holding neighbors off with guns (A2, A6); no killing or lynching of the victim is reported.

Two differently worded dispatches from Harmony Grove, the Constitution special (A6, copied in A2, A11) and the 'Lynching Party on the Trail' wire (A1, A10), agree on the three named white men and the assault on the woman, though neither is a local follow-up and no arrest or court report was found.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution special from Harmony Grove
accounts.gist: Three young white men broke into a Black home, threw the baby from the mother's arms, held her in a field for two hours while armed against neighbors, and left her helpless; they were said to be drunk, and warrants were out.

accounts.label: 'Lynching Party on the Trail' wire
accounts.gist: Posses of both blacks and whites were searching for the three men, charged with torturing and criminally assaulting the woman, and lynching was openly said to await their capture.

accounts.label: Manning Times rewrite
accounts.gist: The men forced the woman at gunpoint into a nearby field and criminally assaulted her; no break-in or baby is mentioned.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Three White Men Outrage Woman' and 'Horrible Crime Is Charged' over a text calling it 'one of the most horrible crimes ever committed in this section'.
The South Carolina and Florida weeklies ran the dispatch as 'Dragged Woman From Home' without comment.
The Manning Times headed its rewrite 'Ought to Be Hung'.
The Springfield Republican said the case showed 'the crime' was not confined to Black men and called for 'the orderly severity of the law' over mob violence.
The Alexandria Gazette's 'Lynching Party on the Trail' reported the lynching threat against the white men as a plain fact.
The Appeal, the Gazette ('White Brutes', 'one of our women') and the Searchlight turned the case against the charge that Black men were peculiarly given to assault.

conflicts.note: Reprinting papers redated the same text; the Constitution special (Nov. 23) is the earliest, and all versions place the attack on the preceding Saturday.

A Black home about 3 miles below Harmony Grove; the woman was taken about 100 yards into a field
An unnamed young Black mother (a 'negress', 'negro woman'); the house held two women and one man, and her baby was thrown from her arms

Three young white men named Chandler, McGinnis and Fitzpatrick (also spelled Fitchpatrick, McGennis)
